lessons.title: Past, present and future
objectives: Use the words past, present and future correctly
Sort things into old and new

keywords.def: things that have already happened
what is happening now
things that have not happened yet
made or used a long time ago

starter: What did you eat for breakfast today?
What do you think you will do tomorrow?

teach.heading: Bismillah: what is history?
bullets: History is the story of the past
The past is what has already happened
Today we learn to be history detectives
teach.note: Begin with bismillah. Ask: has anyone been a detective before? Explain that historians look for clues to find out what life was like long ago.

teach.heading: Past, present, future
teach.note: Hold up three cards (yesterday, today, tomorrow). Pupils point to the right card as you say a sentence, e.g. 'I ate my lunch an hour ago'. Misconception: 'the past' only means a very long time ago; an hour ago is also the past.

teach.heading: Old and new objects
bullets: A telephone with a cord is old
Old things can show us the past
teach.note: Show two pictures: a landline telephone with a curly cord and a mobile phone. Ask which one grandparents used when they were children. Praise the words 'old' and 'new'.

teach.heading: Words that help us
bullets: Long ago, a long time ago
teach.note: Practise the vocabulary with actions: pupils point behind them for 'past', in front for 'future', down for 'now'.

practice: Teacher says: 'We ate breakfast.' Is that past, present or future?
Teacher says: 'We are on Teams now.' Is that past, present or future?
Teacher says: 'We will go to bed tonight.' Is that past, present or future?
independent: Draw one thing you did yesterday, one thing you are doing now and one thing you will do tomorrow
Label your three drawings past, present and future
Say one sentence about your picture using the word 'yesterday'
exit: Is yesterday the past, present or future?
Is a mobile phone old or new?
lessons.homework: Ask a grown-up at home to show you one old object and one new object, and tell the class about them next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: use picture cards and gestures for past, present, future and accept pointing as an answer. Stretch: add the words 'last week' and 'next week' to the sorting.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Childhood within living memory (Memory Box)
lessons.title: My own timeline
lessons.bigQuestion: How have you changed since you were a baby?
objectives: To understand how a timeline shows the order of our life
successCriteria: All: order three pictures from baby to now
Most: use before, after and now
Some: say one way you have changed
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: thanking Allah for growing and learning

keywords.def: a line that shows things in time order
a very young child
a small child learning to walk
earlier
later
at this time

hook.text: What could you do as a baby? What can you do now?

islamicLink.text: Allah says He created us weak, then gave us strength (Ar-Rum 30:54). We were babies who could do nothing, and now we can walk, talk and learn the Qur'an. We thank Allah for each stage.

starter.q: Which is a material: wood or a cat?
The first person on the Moon was Neil ...

teach.heading: Life in order
bullets: Each comes after the one before
teach.note: Use objects, not people: a baby bottle, small shoes, a school bag.

teach.heading: Time words
teach.note: Model: 'Before I could walk, I crawled. Now I can run.'

teach.heading: How I changed
teach.note: Ask: what can you do now that you could not do as a baby?

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: We are babies first, then toddlers, then children.

practice.q: Put in order: child, baby, toddler.
practice.model:
Who is youngest? The baby.
Who walks next? The toddler.
Who goes to school? The child.
Baby, toddler, child.

practice.q: Finish: Before I could walk, I ...

practice.a: For example: read, run, say Al-Fatihah

independent.q: Core: Draw three things on your timeline: a baby bottle, small shoes, your school bag. Write baby, toddler, now.
independent.a: Three pictures in order with labels
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: bottle on the left, shoes in the middle, bag on the right; writes the three labels.

independent.a: For example: Now I can ride a bike

independent.q: Stretch: What will you be able to do next year?

exit.q: Big question: how have you changed since you were a baby?
exit.a: For example: I am taller and I can talk, read and pray

lessons.homework: Put five photos of yourself in order with your family and talk about the changes (keep the photos at home; do not upload them).
lessons.send: SEND: three picture cards to order. EAL: before, after, now with pictures. Stretch: add years to the timeline.

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Childhood within living memory (Memory Box)
lessons.title: Toys long ago and today
lessons.bigQuestion: Would a toy from long ago still be fun today?
objectives: To understand how toys have changed within living memory
successCriteria: All: say if a toy is old or new
Most: say what an old toy is made of
Some: give one way toys have changed
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: materials (wood, metal, plastic) from Spring 1
lessons.smsc: Social: respect for elders and their memories

keywords.def: an object from the past
made a long time ago
made recently
what people alive now can remember
the parent of your mum or dad

hook.text: What toy would your grandparent have played with when they were six?

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches us to honour our elders. Asking grandparents about their childhood is a kind way to spend time with them and learn from them.

starter.q: Which comes first: baby or toddler?

teach.heading: What is an artefact?
bullets: It tells us about life then
We look closely and ask questions
teach.note: Hold up an object. Ask: is it old or new? How can we tell?

teach.heading: Old toys
teach.note: Many toys long ago were wood, metal or cloth. Show photos of objects only.

teach.heading: Toys today
teach.note: Many toys today are plastic. Some need batteries or a screen.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: A wooden spinning top is most likely:
check.why: Wooden tops were common long ago. Some new ones are still made, so we look for other clues.

practice.q: Old or new: a tablet game?
practice.model:
Does it need a battery or a screen?
Yes.
Screens are new.
So it is new.

practice.q: What is a wooden top made of?
Old or new: marbles in a cloth bag?
practice.a: Old (they are still played today too)

independent.q: Core: Sort six toy pictures into 'long ago' and 'today'.
independent.a: Long ago: wooden top, marbles, skipping rope; today: tablet game, plastic robot, remote-control car
independent.model: Teacher does the first card: wooden top, made of wood, no battery, goes in 'long ago'.

independent.q: Extend: Write what one old toy is made of.
independent.a: For example: The top is made of wood

independent.q: Stretch: Which toy would you choose and why?

exit.q: Big question: would a toy from long ago still be fun today?
exit.a: For example: yes, a spinning top is still fun because you can race it

lessons.homework: Find an old object at home and ask who used it and when.
lessons.send: SEND: real objects to hold and sort. EAL: old and new with pictures. Stretch: put three toys in order from oldest to newest.
resources: Tarbiyyah Primary Year 1 curriculum map and long-term plans 2023-24; TGA Year 1 Curriculum Pack, Topic, Spring 2 Memory Box (companion: Human Senses) (Cornerstones Maestro: CHECK IN MAESTRO)
Toy sorting cards, six pictures of objects (portal printable)
Any old object at home (with an adult's permission)

lessons.unit: Spring 2: Childhood within living memory (Memory Box)
lessons.title: Asking an elder about the past
lessons.bigQuestion: What question would you most like to ask your grandparent about when they were young?
objectives: To understand how asking older people questions helps us learn about the past
successCriteria: All: ask one question about the past
Some: compare their answer with life now
lessons.crossCurricular: English: writing questions with question marks
lessons.smsc: Moral: adab with elders, listening and thanking

keywords.def: something we ask to find out
asking someone questions and listening
in the past
at this time
when something becomes different

hook.text: What is the oldest thing you know about your family?

islamicLink.text: The Prophet ﷺ taught us to show mercy to the young and respect to the old. Listening to our elders is part of good manners in Islam.

starter.q: An artefact is an object from the ...
Many old toys were made of:

starter.a: Sight, hearing, touch, taste or smell

teach.heading: Question words
teach.note: Model a question: 'What games did you play?'

teach.heading: Good interview manners
teach.note: Adab: speak gently and listen to elders.

teach.heading: Plan three questions
bullets: How did you talk to friends far away?
teach.note: Pupils choose or change the questions.

teach.heading: Then and now
teach.note: Many grandparents wrote letters. Now we can video call.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.why: A question asks something and ends with a question mark.

practice.a: For example: Where did you go to school?
practice.model:
Start with 'Where'.
Add the idea: go to school.
End with a question mark.
Where did you go to school?

practice.q: What do we say after the interview?

independent.q: Core: Write three questions to ask a family elder on the question sheet.
independent.model: Teacher writes question 1 first: 'What games did you play?'

independent.q: Extend: Guess one answer your elder might give.
independent.a: For example: they played marbles outside

independent.q: Stretch: Write one question about a change.
independent.a: For example: What is different now?

exit.q: Big question: what would you most like to ask your grandparent?
exit.a: Any good question with a question word

lessons.homework: Interview an older relative using your three questions; draw or write one answer to share next lesson (a phone call or video call is fine).
lessons.send: SEND: question starters on cards. EAL: what, where, when with pictures. Stretch: write a fourth question about the masjid long ago.

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Neil Armstrong and the Moon landing (Moon Zoom!)
lessons.title: Neil Armstrong and the first Moon landing
lessons.bigQuestion: How do we know that people walked on the Moon?
objectives: To understand who Neil Armstrong was and why the 1969 Moon landing is remembered
successCriteria: All: say that Neil Armstrong was the first person on the Moon
Most: say that it happened in 1969, long ago
Some: name one source that tells us about it
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the Moon is made of rock
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the Moon as a sign of Allah

keywords.def: a person trained to travel into space
the big rock that goes round the Earth
a machine that flies into space
the year people first walked on the Moon
something that tells us about the past

hook.text: If you went to the Moon, what would you bring back to show your family?

islamicLink.text: Allah made the Moon and gave it phases so that we can count the months and years (Yunus 10:5). Muslims watch for the new Moon to start each month, like Ramadan. People who visited the Moon saw one of Allah's great signs close up.

starter.q: Is 'long ago' in the past or the future?
What is in the sky at night that changes shape?
Name one old object your family has.
starter.a: For example: an old photo or a watch

teach.heading: A trip to the Moon
bullets: In 1969 three astronauts flew to the Moon
teach.note: The rocket was a Saturn V. It took off from Florida in the USA on 16 July 1969.

teach.heading: Neil Armstrong
bullets: The first person to walk on the Moon
Michael Collins flew round the Moon
teach.note: We do not show pictures of the astronauts. Show the footprint photo. Ask: what made this?

teach.heading: How do we know?
teach.note: These are sources. Grandparents or great-grandparents may remember watching it on television.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Who was first to walk on the Moon?
check.why: Neil Armstrong was first. Buzz Aldrin was second. Michael Collins stayed in the spacecraft.

practice.q: In what year did people first walk on the Moon?
practice.model:
Look at the timeline.
The landing was on 20 July 1969.
So the year is 1969.

practice.q: What did the astronauts bring back?
Was 1969 long ago or last week?

independent.q: Core: Draw the rocket and the Moon. Write 'Neil Armstrong 1969'.
independent.a: A drawing of a rocket and the Moon with the label
independent.model: Teacher shows it first: a tall rocket, the round grey Moon, and the words 'Neil Armstrong 1969'.

independent.q: Extend: Plan one question to ask an older relative about the Moon landing.
independent.a: For example: Did you see it on television?

independent.q: Stretch: Name one source that shows the Moon landing happened.
independent.a: Photos, Moon rocks or people's memories

exit.q: Big question: how do we know that people walked on the Moon?

lessons.homework: Ask an older relative what they know about the 1969 Moon landing and tell the class next lesson.
lessons.send: SEND: picture timeline to order (rocket, Moon, splashdown). EAL: astronaut, rocket, Moon with pictures. Stretch: order three events on a timeline.

lessons.unit: Summer 1: The Great Fire of London, 1666 (Bright Lights, Big City)
lessons.title: The Great Fire of London, 1666
lessons.bigQuestion: How did one small fire in a bakery burn down most of a city?
objectives: To understand why the Great Fire of London spread and how we know about it
successCriteria: All: say where and when the fire started
Most: give one reason the fire spread
Some: say how Samuel Pepys' diary helps us
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: next week we test why wood burns and brick does not

keywords.def: the year of the Great Fire of London
the street where the fire began
a person who makes bread
a book where someone writes what happens each day
clues that tell us what happened

hook.text: What could make a fire spread from one house to the next?

starter.q: A long time ago is the:

starter.a: For example: Tower Bridge, London Eye, St Paul's Cathedral

teach.heading: London in 1666
teach.note: Show a drawing of the old wooden houses (buildings only). Ask: what might happen if one caught fire?

teach.heading: The fire starts
bullets: Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane
It burned for about four days
teach.note: The baker's oven fire started it in the night.

teach.heading: Why it spread
bullets: The summer was hot and dry
teach.note: People used leather buckets and pulled houses down with hooks to stop it.

teach.heading: How do we know?
bullets: He saw the fire and wrote about it
He buried his cheese to save it!
teach.note: A diary is evidence. Pepys really did bury his parmesan cheese and wine in his garden.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share the results.

check.q: The Great Fire started in a:
check.why: It began in Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane.

practice.q: When did the Great Fire start?
practice.model:
I look at the title.
It says the Great Fire of London, 1666.
So it started in 1666.

practice.q: Name one thing that helped the fire spread.
practice.a: Wind, dry weather or wooden houses

independent.q: Core: Put four pictures in order: the bakery, the fire spreading, the buckets, the new brick houses. Draw buildings and flames only.
independent.a: 1 bakery, 2 fire spreading, 3 buckets and fire hooks, 4 new brick houses
independent.model: Teacher shows which comes first: the bakery, where it all began.

independent.q: Extend: Write a caption for picture 2.
independent.a: For example: The wind blew the fire from house to house.

independent.q: Stretch: Why is a diary good evidence?

exit.q: Big question: how did one small fire burn most of a city?
exit.a: Wind and dry weather blew it from wooden house to wooden house

lessons.homework: Retell the story of the Great Fire to your family using your four pictures in the right order.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards to order with a word bank. EAL: fire, wind, wood, bakery with pictures. Stretch: find out what the Monument in London is for.
